source_metadata.title: Prehospital Injury Severity Estimate (PHISE) matches in-hospital trauma scores when embedded in AI models

extraction_limitations: Supplementary material was referenced by the article but was not included in the uploaded PDF; atoms that cite supplementary benchmark results rely only on values reported in the main-text discussion.
The article contains an internal model-name inconsistency: the detailed derivation section identifies GPT-4o-mini (April 2025), whereas a later Methods paragraph refers more generically to GPT-4.

The article describes the TraumaRegister DGU evaluation as prospective in the Introduction but describes the overall study as retrospective and registry-based in Methods using previously anonymized extracts; atoms avoid assigning a prospective design label to the analyzed external cohort.
The NTDB median-age IQR is inconsistent between narrative Results (50 years, IQR 26–69) and Table 1 (50 years, IQR 29–69); no age-distribution atom was emitted.

Table 1 reports mortality/transfusion counts alongside percentages that are not simple fractions of the full cohort N, implying outcome-specific denominators or missingness that are not explicitly shown; atoms preserve the reported percentages without calculating denominators.

Figure 5 labels an imaging-score comparator as ISS/NISS-based; individual NISS model metrics are not separately displayed in the main-text figure, so the ML comparator atoms preserve the figure-level combined labeling rather than inventing separate NISS values.
Operational performance, interrater reliability, time burden, workflow integration, and clinical impact were explicitly not tested; no atom converts proposed use cases into demonstrated outcomes.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study tested whether a simplified region-based injury severity score based only on clinically accessible scene information could approximate ISS/NISS performance.
The investigators evaluated PHISE in NTDB and TraumaRegister DGU data and embedded PHISE, ISS, and NISS into machine-learning models with prehospital variables to compare outcome prediction.
PHISE uses eight body regions: head, face/neck, thorax/chest, abdomen, pelvis, upper extremity, lower extremity, and spine.
PHISE grades each body region on a four-level scale from 0 (no injury) to 3 (severe injury).
AIS severities were mapped to PHISE as AIS 0→0, AIS 1→1, AIS 2–3→2, and AIS 4–6→3.
Patient-level PHISE was calculated by summing the squares of the three highest PHISE regional severity scores.
The authors state that PHISE is intended to complement physiological assessment and clinical judgment rather than replace them.
The NTDB source population included 1,097,190 trauma patients reported to the 2019 NTDB before derivation-cohort exclusions.

population.label: NTDB 2019 source population before derivation exclusions

atoms.canonical_statement: After excluding unmappable AIS entries or missing key prehospital variables, 397,864 patients remained in the NTDB derivation cohort.
The external validation cohort comprised 14,136 TraumaRegister DGU patients from Germany, Switzerland, and Austria.
NTDB patients were included when anatomical injury coding was complete and ISS/NISS plus core demographic and prehospital data were available.

population.label: NTDB eligibility
inclusion_criteria: Complete AIS-defined injury coding and complete ISS/NISS calculation
Core demographic and prehospital data available

atoms.canonical_statement: AIS-coded injury descriptions were submitted to ChatGPT GPT-4o-mini (April 2025) to classify whether diagnosis could be approximated clinically, required imaging, or was undetermined.
The imaging-need prompt was executed three times on identical inputs, disagreements were resolved by majority vote, and outputs were manually spot-checked for face validity.
Rule-based NLP mapped AIS-coded body regions to the eight PHISE body regions.

Injuries judged imaging-dependent or undetermined were assigned random PHISE severity grades to simulate prehospital uncertainty; the later Methods section states these assignments were based on frequency distributions.

External validation used a routinely recorded simplified prehospital injury score in TraumaRegister DGU that the authors considered compatible with PHISE, although it retained external soft-tissue injury as a separate region.

atoms.canonical_statement: The investigators tested logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, XGBoost, AdaBoost, LightGBM, naïve Bayes, and multilayer perceptron models; XGBoost was selected as best-performing and suitable.
Before model training, the derivation cohort was randomly split 80%/20% into training and internal validation sets.
Missing continuous values were mean-imputed, ordinal values median-imputed, categorical values mode-imputed, and features were scaled with scikit-learn ColumnTransformer.
Model fitting used nested cross-validation with hyperparameter tuning and 10-fold cross-validation; performance metrics were calculated with a 1000-fold bootstrap.

Multivariable XGBoost prognostic models used one injury-severity score (ISS, NISS, or PHISE) plus prehospital age, sex, GCS, injury mechanism, and vital signs; models were trained on NTDB and tested on TraumaRegister DGU.
SHAP values were used for model interpretation, with feature importances scaled between 0 and 1 and ranked by mean global importance on the validation split.
The PHISE-based XGBoost mortality model had ROC AUC 0.90.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors report that PHISE-based ML models outperformed rSIG and TRISS in both benchmark scenarios.

The authors conclude that PHISE is a complementary imaging-free anatomical input for early trauma stratification and that adding prehospital physiology and mechanism narrows the performance gap versus ISS/NISS-based models.

The authors propose potential uses for PHISE in AI-enhanced dispatch, early transfusion protocols, direct-to-operating-room routing, and ICU resource planning, while framing these as opportunities rather than validated clinical effects.

PHISE primarily captures anatomical injury burden and does not fully account for physiological response, frailty, comorbidity, or disproportionate effects of severe isolated traumatic brain or spinal cord injury.
PHISE accuracy depends on examiner experience and the quality of prehospital documentation because it relies on clinical examination and scene assessment.
Subtle or occult injuries may be missed by prehospital PHISE assessment.

Operationality, interrater reliability, time burden, workflow integration, and clinical impact were not assessed, and the authors state that prospective EMS validation is required before routine implementation.
The NTDB is a voluntary hospital-reported registry dominated by Level I and II trauma centers and may overrepresent higher-resourced institutions.
AIS 2005 versus AIS 2015 severity differences were found in 45 injury codes, representing 2.4% of reviewed injury codes.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study states that it followed TRIPOD+AI reporting guidance and used anonymized/de-identified registry data under institutional ethical oversight; informed consent was waived for the retrospective anonymized analyses.
NTDB data can be purchased from the American College of Surgeons, while TraumaRegister DGU extracts may be requested from the corresponding author subject to DGU approval and ethical approval.
R and Python code used to reproduce the figures is available from the authors upon request rather than in a public repository.
Open-access funding was enabled and organized by Projekt DEAL; M.S. also acknowledged research support from the Joachim Herz Foundation.
The authors declared no competing interests.
